newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania returns Germany's wartime embassy building.
newsitem.headline: Romania returns Germany's wartime embassy building.

text.p: Romanian President Emil Constantinescu approved on Tuesday a government move to return to the German government its former Bucharest embassy, seized by the communists after World War Two.
Constantinescu's office said he had signed into law a government ruling, approved by parliament, to return the building, which houses one of the poshest of Bucharest's dozens of casinos.

"The building which housed the German embassy in Romania until 1944 is being transferred free of charge to the property of the Federal Republic of Germany," says the law, which comes into effect upon publication in the Official Gazette.

The centrist government, which ousted ex-communists in elections last year, has been at pains to improve ties with Bonn to secure support for its bid to gain membership of NATO and the European Union. Romania has been told it must wait for entry into both organisations.

A German embassy official said the government was grateful for the return of the building and would discuss details of the transfer. The turn-of-the-century building features in several World War Two works of fiction describing Nazi occupation.
It functioned as a music-hall theatre until the 1989 fall of communism. "Now there's a casino, and we're respecting the lease which expires in 2002," the German embassy official said.
Romania switched from its wartime alliance with Hitler's Germany to join the Allied side in August 1944 as the Red Army began moving through the country on its way to capture Berlin.

Foreign Minister Adrian Severin apologised to Germany earlier this year for the post-war deportation of tens of thousands of ethnic Germans to Soviet labour camps and for their Communist-era "sale" for cash to Bonn in exchange for emigration permits.
Around 800,000 Germans lived in Romania before World War Two, as well as an equal number of Jews. Mass emigration to Germany has reduced the German community to about 70,000.
Its Jewish population was halved during the Nazi Holocaust. Only 14,000 mainly elderly Jews remain.
Romanian authorities are only just beginning to restore property to the Jewish community, including hundreds of synagogues, former hospitals, ritual baths and other buildings.
